source_text: Ἔξεστι δὲ ἡμῖν ἐκ περιουσίας πρὸς τοὺς φιλεγκλήμονας ἐπαποδύσασθαι· οὐ γὰρ παῖδες ἡμεῖς καὶ νήπιοι πρὸς τὸ παιδαριῶδες καὶ εὐκαταφρόνητον τῆς μαθήσεως προσηγορεύμεθα, καθὼς οἱ εἰς γνῶσιν πεφυσιωμένοι διαβεβλήκασιν· ἀναγεννηθέντες γοῦν εὐθέως τὸ τέλειον ἀπειλήφαμεν, οὗ ἕνεκεν ἐσπεύδομεν. ἐφωτίσθημεν γάρ· τὸ δὲ ἔστιν ἐπιγνῶναι τὸν θεόν. οὔκουν ἀτελὴς ὁ ἐγνωκὼς τὸ τέλειον. καί μου μὴ λάβησθε ὁμολογοῦντος ἐγνωκέναι τὸν θεόν. ὧδέ πως γὰρ ἔδοξεν εἰπεῖν τῷ λόγῳ· ὃ δὲ ἐλεύθερος. αὐτίκα γοῦν βαπτιζομένῳ τῷ κυρίῳ ἀπ᾿ οὐρανῶν ἐπήχησε φωνὴ μάρτυς ἠγαπημένου »υἱός μου εἶ σὺ ἀγαπητός, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε.« πυθώμεθα οὖν τῶν σοφῶν· σήμερον ἀναγεννηθεὶς ὁ Χριστὸς ἤδη τέλειός ἐστιν ἤ, ὅπερ ἀτοπώτατον, ἐλλιπής. εἰ δὲ τοῦτο, προσμαθεῖν τι αὐτῷ δεῖ. ἀλλὰ προσμαθεῖν μὲν αὐτὸν εἰκὸς οὐδὲ ἓν θεὸν ὄντα. οὐ γὰρ ἂν μείζων τις εἴη τοῦ λόγου οὐδὲ μὴν διδάσκαλος τοῦ μόνου διδασκάλου. μή τι οὖν ὁμολογήσουσιν ἄκοντες τὸν λόγον, τέλειον ἐκ τελείου φύντα τοῦ πατρός, κατὰ τὴν οἰκονομικὴν προδιατύπωσιν ἀναγεννηθῆναι τελείως; καὶ εἰ τέλειος ἦν, τί ἐβαπτίζετο ὁ τέλειος; ἔδει, φασί, πληρῶσαι τὸ ἐπάγγελμα τὸ ἀνθρώπινον. παγκάλως. φημὶ γάρ· ἅμα τοίνυν τῷ βαπτίζεσθαι αὐτὸν ὑπὸ Ἰωάννου γίνεται τέλειος; δῆλον ὅτι. οὐδὲν οὖν πρὸς αὐτοῦ προσέμαθεν; οὐ γάρ. τελειοῦται δὲ τῷ λουτρῷ μόνῳ καὶ τοῦ πνεύματος τῇ καθόδῳ ἁγιάζεται; οὕτως ἔχει. Τὸ δὲ αὐτὸ συμβαίνει τοῦτο καὶ περὶ ἡμᾶς, ὧν γέγονεν ὑπογραφὴ ὁ κύριος· βαπτιζόμενοι φωτιζόμεθα, φωτιζόμενοι υἱοποιούμεθα, υἱοποιούμενοι τελειούμεθα, τελειούμενοι ἀπαθανατιζόμεθα »ἐγώ«, φησίν, »εἶπα, θεοί ἐστε καὶ υἱοὶ ὑψίστου πάντες.« καλεῖται δὲ πολλαχῶς τὸ ἔργον τοῦτο, χάρισμα καὶ φώτισμα καὶ τέλειον καὶ λουτρόν· λουτρὸν μὲν δι᾿ οὗ τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἀπορρυπτόμεθα, χάρισμα δὲ ᾧ τὰ ἐπὶ τοῖς ἁμαρτήμασιν ἐπιτίμια ἀνεῖται, φώτισμα δὲ δι᾿ οὗ τὸ ἅγιον ἐκεῖνο φῶς τὸ σωτήριον ἐποπτεύεται, τουτέστιν δι᾿ οὗ τὸ θεῖον ὀξυωποῦμεν, τέλειον δὲ τὸ ἀπροσδεὲς φαμέν. τί γὰρ ἔτι λείπεται τῷ θεὸν ἐγνωκότι; καὶ γὰρ ἄτοπον ὡς ἀληθῶς χάρισμα κεκλῆσθαι θεοῦ τὸ μὴ πεπληρωμένον· τέλειος δὲ ὢν τέλεια χαριεῖται δήπουθεν· ὡς δὲ ἅμα τῷ κελεῦσαι αὐτὸν πάντα γίνεται, οὕτως ἕπεται τῷ χαρίσασθαι μόνον βουληθῆναι αὐτὸν τὸ πεπληρῶσθαι τὴν χάριν. τὸ γὰρ μέλλον τοῦ χρόνου τῇ δυνάμει τοῦ θελήματος προλαμβάνεται. πρὸς δὲ καὶ ἡ τῶν κακῶν ἀπαλλαγὴ σωτηρίας ἐστὶν ἀρχή. μόνον δὲ ἄρα οἱ πρῶτον δραξάμενοι τῶν ὅρων τῆς ζωῆς ἤδη τέλειοι, ζῶμεν δὲ ἤδη οἱ θανάτου κεχωρισμένοι. σωτηρία τοίνυν τὸ ἕπεσθαι Χριστῷ. »ὃ γὰρ γέγονεν ἐν αὐτῷ, ζωή ἐστιν.« »ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν,« φησίν, »ὁ τὸν λόγον μου ἀκούων καὶ πιστεύων τῷ πέμψαντί με ἔχει ζωὴν αἰώνιον καὶ εἰς κρίσιν οὐκ ἔρχεται, ἀλλὰ μεταβέβηκεν ἐκ τοῦ θανάτου εἰς τὴν ζωήν.« οὕτω τὸ πιστεῦσαι μόνον καὶ ἀναγεννηθῆναι τελείωσίς ἐστιν ἐν ζωῇ· οὐ γάρ ποτε ἀσθενεῖ ὁ θεός.
pass_a_gloss: It is possible for us to divest ourselves of superfluity towards those who love to be stripped; for we are not children and infants in respect to the childish and easily despised learning, as those who have been brought to knowledge have slandered; for having been reborn, we immediately received the perfect, on account of which we hasten. For we have been enlightened; and this is to know God. Therefore, the one who has known the perfect is not imperfect. And do not take hold of me as I confess to having known God. For thus it seemed right to the Word to speak; and what is free. Immediately, therefore, to the Lord being baptized from heaven, a voice sounded as a witness, 'You are my beloved Son, today I have begotten you.' Let us learn from the wise; today, having been reborn, is Christ already perfect or, what is most absurd, imperfect? But if this, it is necessary for him to learn something. But it is not likely that he, being God, would learn even one thing. For no one would be greater than the Word, nor even a teacher of the only Teacher. Will they not, therefore, involuntarily confess the Word, perfect from the perfect Father, to have been reborn perfectly according to the economic pre-arrangement? And if he was perfect, why was the perfect one baptized? It was necessary, they say, to fulfill the human promise. Beautifully, I say; for as soon as he was baptized by John, did he become perfect? Clearly. Did he, therefore, learn nothing in addition to this? No. Is he perfected by the bath alone and sanctified by the descent of the Spirit? It holds thus. The same thing happens to us, of whom the Lord has become a guarantee; being baptized, we are enlightened, being enlightened, we are made sons, being made sons, we are perfected, being perfected, we are made immortal. 'I said', he says, 'you are gods and all sons of the Most High.' And this work is called by many names, a gift and enlightenment and perfection and bath; a bath, indeed, through which we wash away sins, a gift, by which the penalties for sins are remitted, enlightenment, through which that holy and saving light is beheld, that is, through which we perceive the divine, perfection, we say, is what is lacking in nothing. For what is still lacking to the one who has known God? And it is also absurd, indeed, for the gift of God to be called imperfect; but being perfect, he will surely give perfect gifts; just as all things come into being as soon as he commands, so also it follows that when he gives, it is only necessary for him to will that the gift be fulfilled. For the future is anticipated by the power of his will. And besides, the removal of evils is the beginning of salvation. Only, therefore, those who have first grasped the boundaries of life are already perfect, and we, having been separated from death, are already living. Salvation, therefore, is to follow Christ. 'For what has come into being in him is life.' 'Amen, amen, I say to you', he says, 'the one who hears my word and believes in the one who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life.' Thus, to believe alone and to be reborn is perfection in life; for God is never weak.
pass_b_english: We can certainly shed our excess baggage when interacting with those who are eager to let go of theirs. As people who have been reborn, we're not naive or immature when it comes to spiritual growth, despite what some critics might say. From the moment we're reborn, we receive the perfect, and that's what drives us forward. Our enlightenment is, in fact, our knowledge of God. So, if we've come to know the perfect, we can't be considered imperfect. I'm not afraid to admit that I've experienced this knowledge of God for myself. The Word has shown us that this is the path to freedom. When the Lord was baptized, a voice from heaven declared, 'You are my beloved Son, today I have begotten you' (Matthew 3:17). Let's consider the implications: if Christ was reborn, was he already perfect, or was he somehow imperfect? If he was imperfect, then he would need to learn and grow. But how could God, the all-knowing and all-powerful one, possibly learn anything new? No one is greater than the Word, and no one can teach the one who is the ultimate Teacher. Won't they have to acknowledge, even if reluctantly, that the Word is perfect, coming from the perfect Father, and that he was reborn in a state of perfection, according to the divine plan? And if he was already perfect, why did he need to be baptized? Some might say it was necessary to fulfill a human obligation. But I say, if he was baptized by John, did that make him perfect? Of course, it did. Did he gain some new knowledge or insight through this experience? Not at all. Was he perfected by the baptism alone, and sanctified by the Holy Spirit's descent? That's exactly what happened. The same process applies to us, who have the Lord as our guarantee. When we're baptized, we're enlightened; when we're enlightened, we become children of God; when we become children of God, we're perfected; and when we're perfected, we become immortal. As the Scripture says, 'I have said, you are gods and all sons of the Most High' (Psalm 82:6). This transformative work can be described in many ways: as a gift, as enlightenment, as perfection, or as a bath. Through this bath, we wash away our sins; through this gift, our penalties are forgiven; through this enlightenment, we behold the holy and saving light, and we come to understand the divine. Perfection, to us, means lacking nothing. What more could we possibly need if we've come to know God? It's absurd to think that God's gift could be imperfect; if God is perfect, then the gifts he gives must also be perfect. Just as everything comes into being when God commands it, so too does the fulfillment of his gifts depend on his will. The future is anticipated by the power of his will. Moreover, the removal of evil is the beginning of salvation. Only those who have grasped the essence of life are already perfect, and we, having been separated from death, are already living. Salvation, therefore, means following Christ. As the Scripture says, 'What has come into being in him is life' (John 5:24). Christ himself says, 'Amen, amen, I say to you, the one who hears my word and believes in the one who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life.' So, to believe and be reborn is to achieve perfection in life; and we can trust that God is always strong and never weak.
